chapters.name: Prehistoric Age and Sources of Ancient Indian History
topics: Purashanakal (Palaeolithic) vs Navapashanakal (Neolithic/Navapashanik) differences
Archaeological sources — inscriptions, monuments, ruins, coins, sculptures, pottery
Literary sources — Vedas, epics (Ramayana/Mahabharata), Puranas, Buddhist/Jain texts
Foreign accounts — Megasthenes (Indika), Al-Biruni (Kitab-ul-Hind), Ibn Battuta (Rihla), Bernier
Inscriptions — oldest inscriptions in Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts
James Prinsep — first to decipher Brahmi script (1837)
Coins — importance in knowing Indian history
Prayag Prashasti — composed by Harisena (about Samudragupta)

chapters.name: Saraswati-Sindhu (Harappan) Civilization and Vedic Age
topics: Discovery — Harappa by Daya Ram Sahni (1921), Mohenjodaro by R.D. Banerjee (1922)
Major Harappan sites — Harappa (Punjab Pakistan), Mohenjodaro (Sindh), Kalibangan (Rajasthan), Lothal (Gujarat — dockyard), Dholavira (Gujarat), Banawali (Haryana), Rangpur (Gujarat)
Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture — found in Khetri area
Town planning — grid pattern (streets at right angles), drainage system, Great Bath
Great Bath — Mohenjodaro mein mila; town planning ka prateek
Harappan script — enigmatic, boustrophedon style, undeciphered to this day
Seals and sealings — trade, identity, religious purposes
Materials for beads — carnelian (lal pathar), steatite, gold, copper, shell
Faience pots — artificial glazed material, ceremonial use
Saddle querns — stone grinders for grain
Agriculture evidence — ploughed field at Kalibangan and Banawali
Weights — made of chert (agate) stone, standardized
Decline of Harappan civilization — various theories (flood, aridity, earthquake)
Canal traces found in Harappan site Shortugai (Afghanistan)
Vedic Age — Rigveda oldest, compiled 1500-1000 BCE
Varna-Ashrama system — four varnas (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra), four ashrams
Exchange medium in Vedic age — Nishka (gold ornament), cattle
Jataka kathas — related to Gautam Buddha's previous lives

chapters.name: Major Ancient Indian Dynasties
topics: Mahajanapadas — 16 in number, emerged 6th century BCE, mostly ruled by Kshatriyas, some oligarchies
Magadha — most powerful Mahajanpad, reasons for rise
Magadha early capitals — Rajagriha/Rajgir (early), Pataliputra (later, on Ganga)
Mauryan Empire — Chandragupta Maurya (founder), Bindusara, Ashoka
Ashoka — most famous Buddhist ruler; adopted Buddhism after Kalinga war
Ashoka's Dhamma — non-violence, tolerance, reverence for elders, service, truth
Dhamma Mahamattas — officers appointed by Ashoka to spread Dhamma
Ashoka's personal religion was Buddhism but Dhamma was universal
Sanchi Stupa — built by Ashoka; preserved by Begums of Bhopal
Post-Mauryan period — kingship concepts: devputra (Kushanas), devanam priya
Gupta period — Samudragupta (Allahabad Prashasti), Chandragupta II
Arthashastra — by Kautilya/Chanakya (NOT Megasthenes — common T/F trap!)
Megasthenes — wrote Indika (about Mauryan India), Greek ambassador
Prayag Prashasti — by Harisena about Samudragupta
Shrenis (guilds) — merchant/artisan guilds in ancient India; ran like states
Fatalists (Ajivikas under Makkhali Gosala) vs Materialists (Lokayatas/Charvakas)

chapters.name: Northern and Southern Indian Dynasties (Bhakti, Vijayanagara, Chola)
topics: Bhakti movement — emergence, Alvars (Vaishnavism), Nayanars (Shaivism), Tamil South
Nalayira Divya Prabandham — collection of 4000 Tamil Vaishnav hymns by Alvars
Alvars and Nayanars attitude towards caste — challenged caste hierarchy
Virashaiva/Lingayat tradition — founded by Basavanna in Karnataka, 12th century
Vachanas — Lingayat writings against caste
Andal — woman Alvar saint, Vaishnav tradition
Mirabai — poet-saint, Vaishnav Bhakti, princess, devoted to Krishna
Mirabai's guru was Ravidas/Raidas (NOT Kabirdas — common T/F trap!)
Saguna Bhakti — God with form (Vaishnav, Shaiva traditions); Nirguna — formless God (Kabir, Nanak)
Kabir — Nirguna Bhakti, verses compiled in Bijak, Guru Granth Sahib, Panchvani
Chola administration — mandalam (province), ur (village assembly), sabha, nagaram (merchant assembly)
Chola local self-government — ur and sabha; praised by historians
Chola temples — Virupaksha (Pattadakal/Vijayanagara), Brihadeeshwara (Tanjore by Rajraj I)
Vijayanagara Empire — founded 1336 AD by Harihar and Bukka (Sangama dynasty)
Hampi — brought to light by Colin Mackenzie (NOT John Marshall — common confusion)
Krishnadeva Raya — most famous ruler, wrote Amukta Malyada in Telugu
Mahanavami Dibba — platform at Vijayanagara, ritual for Mahanavami festival
Vitthala temple — famous temple, stone chariot, beautiful architecture
Amara Nayaka system — military governors who controlled territory
Water conservation in Vijayanagara — tanks, canals, wells
Battle of Rakshasi-Tangadi (Talikota) — 1565 AD, Vijayanagara defeated by Deccan Sultanates
Agricultural fields incorporated in fortified area — reason: supply during siege
Therigatha — poems by Buddhist women monks

chapters.name: Delhi Sultanate (Travellers, Sufism, Bhakti)
topics: Al-Biruni — Kitab-ul-Hind (comparative method, Sanskrit texts translated); came with Mahmud Ghazni
Al-Biruni's distinctive structure in Kitab-ul-Hind — begins with a theory, then gives Indian and Greek views comparatively
Ibn Battuta — Moroccan, 'Rihla' book, came to India as qazi under Muhammad bin Tughlaq
Ibn Battuta's descriptions — coconut (nar-i-Hind), communication system (postal relay horses), Mughal cities
Bernier — French, came as physician to Dara Shikoh (later Aurangzeb), described Mughal cities as 'Camp Towns'
Bernier's Camp Towns description — because city without emperor moved with emperor's camp
Manucci — Italian, NOT the one who called cities 'Camp Towns' (Bernier did)
Alauddin Khilji — market control policy (4 markets, inspectors, price fixing)
Sufism — Islam mein mystical tradition, emphasized love for God
Chishti order — most popular in India; Shaikh Muinuddin Chishti (Ajmer), Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki (Delhi), Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi)
Khanqah — Sufi lodge/hospice, controlled by Sheikh/Pir
Rulers wanted Sufi support — legitimacy, spiritual blessings
Bhakti movement — Sant tradition, reached north India by 15th-16th century
Khalsa Panth — founded by Guru Gobind Singh (10th Guru), 1699 AD at Anandpur Sahib
Adi Granth Sahib — compiled by Guru Arjan Dev Ji
Nirguna Bhakti — Kabir (caste rejection), Guru Nanak (Sikhism root)
Saguna Bhakti — Mirabai (Krishna), Tukaram, Chaitanya
Nalayira Divya Prabandham — Tamil Vaishnav hymns by Alvars

chapters.name: Mughal Era
topics: Akbar — Mansabdari system (started in India by Akbar), Sulh-i-Kul (peace with all), Din-i-Ilahi
Mansabdari system — zat (personal rank), sawar (cavalry rank); 10 se 5000+ tak; ameer-ul-umara highest
Din-i-Ilahi — Akbar's new religion, combined elements of all religions; died with Akbar
Aurangzeb's Deccan policy — consequences: weakened empire, Maratha rise, treasury empty
Ain-i-Akbari — written by Abul Fazl, 3 parts, administrative details of Akbar's reign
Akbarnama — by Abul Fazl, Akbar's history
Mughal rural community — three constituents: zamindars, peasants (khud-kashta, pahi-kashta), village officials
Khud-kashta — resident peasants who owned land
Pahi-kashta — migrant peasants who cultivated others' land
Polaj — regularly cultivated land (best land)
Parauti — fallow for one or two seasons
Chachar — fallow for 3-4 years
Banjar — long-term fallow (5+ years)
Jins-i-kamil (perfect crops) — cotton and indigo; most profitable
Mawas — difficult/frontier tracts, outlaws and rebels took refuge here
Jama and Hasil in Mughal period — Jama = assessed revenue, Hasil = actual collection
Bernier — compared Mughal cities to camp towns, described sati, criticized Mughal land system
Bernier described sati practice — attracted by tragic element, women's choice vs. social pressure
Jajmani system — hereditary service exchange between castes in villages
Zabt system — method of revenue assessment by Todar Mal under Akbar

chapters.name: Maratha Power (Maratha Shakti)
topics: Rise of Maratha power — causes: geography of Maharashtra, religious awakening (Bhakti movement), guerrilla warfare, weakness of Deccan Sultans, linguistic unity, military experience, Shivaji's leadership
Shivaji — great nation-builder, born 1627; Ashta Pradhan system, Chauth, Sardeshmukhi
Ashta Pradhan — 8 ministers: Peshwa, Amatya, Mantri, Sachiv, Sumant, Senapati, Panditrao, Nyayadhish
Peshwa = Prime Minister (Pradhan Mantri) of Maratha state
Chauth — 1/4th (25%) of revenue collected from conquered areas
Sardeshmukhi — 10% extra revenue collected from entire kingdom
Battle of Haldighati (1576) — Maharana Pratap vs. Akbar's army; Pratap forced to retreat but never surrendered
Maharana Pratap — Sisodiya dynasty, fought lifelong against Mughal subjugation
Dr. Ashirvadilal Srivastava quote on Maratha rise — 200 years of preparation
Shivaji's guerrilla warfare — Mavala soldiers, hill forts strategy
Shivaji's character — skilled military commander, diplomat, administrator, religious tolerant

chapters.name: British Rule in India
topics: Battle of Plassey (1757) — British vs. Siraj-ud-Daula (Bengal Nawab); British won by deceit (Mir Jafar)
Battle of Buxar (1764) — British vs. Mir Kasim + Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II + Nawab of Awadh; British won
Treaty of Allahabad (1765) — terms: Diwani of Bengal, Bihar, Odisha to British; Shah Alam's pension; Awadh returned
Buxar significance > Plassey — Plassey gave indirect control, Buxar gave legal/formal control of India

Land Revenue Systems in India: (1) Permanent Settlement (Bengal, 1793, Cornwallis), (2) Ryotwari (Madras/Bombay, with individual farmers), (3) Mahalwari (Punjab/UP/Gangetic Plains, with village communities)
Fifth Report — submitted to British Parliament in 1813 (NOT 1815 — T/F trap!); about EIC administration
Subsidiary Alliance — started by Wellesley (NOT Cornwallis); rulers had to maintain British troops at their cost
Doctrine of Lapse — by Dalhousie; if no natural heir, state annexed by British
Dalhousie — Doctrine of Lapse; 'A cherry that will drop in our mouth one day' (about Awadh)
Cornwallis — Permanent Settlement in Bengal; Ryotwari system introduced later in Madras by Munro
Taluqdars — large landholders in Awadh; Taluqdar ka shhabdik arth = someone holding taluq (attachment)
Jotedars — powerful village-level landholders in Bengal; more powerful than Zamindars at local level
Zamindars — landholders under Permanent Settlement; had to pay fixed revenue or lose land
Awadh called Nursery of Bengal Army — because most sepoys came from Awadh; annexation 1856 caused resentment
Decline of Portuguese power in India — discipline lack, incompetent successors after Albuquerque, competition from Dutch/British/French
Cotton Supply Association — founded in Britain 1857 to reduce dependence on American cotton
Deccan Riots (1875) — against moneylenders; started in Poona/Indapur district
Sunset Law — land taken away at sunset if revenue not paid; oppressive revenue law

chapters.name: Resistance to British Rule (1857 and Tribal Revolts)
topics: Revolt of 1857 — started 10 May 1857 from Meerut cantonment
Immediate cause — greased cartridges (pig and cow fat; offended both Muslims and Hindus)
Nature of 1857 revolt — debate: mere mutiny vs. first war of independence
John Lawrence, John Seeley — 'merely a military revolt'
V.D. Savarkar, Ashok Mehta — 'first war of Indian independence'
Main leaders of 1857: Rani Lakshmibai (Jhansi), Nana Sahib (Kanpur), Tantya Tope, Kunwar Singh (Bihar/Arrah), Begum Hazrat Mahal (Lucknow), Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah ('Danka Shah')
Rani Lakshmibai — 'Khoob lari mardani' — poem by Subhadra Kumari Chauhan
Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah — called 'Danka Shah' (drum king) for inspiring soldiers
Awadh called Nursery of Bengal Army — reason for revolt intensity there
British repression methods — new laws, disarming rebels, pardoning surrenderers early, military force
1857 revolt failure causes — premature start, limited area, no common goal, lack of resources, lack of organization
Rumours during 1857 revolt — why people believed: flour mixed with bone, cartridges greased, social anxiety
Rebels' unity efforts — appealing to common religion, declaring Bahadur Shah Zafar as leader, pamphlets
Santhal Revolt (1855-56) — against moneylenders, zamindars, British; leaders: Sidhu and Kanhu Manjhi
Santhal revolt causes — exploitation by dikus (outsiders), moneylenders, unfair land settlement
Manzil-abadi — Kanpur (location important for 1857)

chapters.name: National Movement (Rashtriya Andolan)
topics: Indian National Congress founding — 1885, A.O. Hume; initial objectives: protect Indian interests, national unity, NOT independence initially
Lal Bal Pal — Lala Lajpat Rai (Punjab), Bal Gangadhar Tilak (Maharashtra), Bipin Chandra Pal (Bengal) — Garam dal
Rise of extremist ideology causes — economic exploitation, Bengal partition, Lord Curzon's works, famine/plague, worldwide events
Bengal Partition — 1905, Lord Curzon — caused massive Swadeshi movement
Gandhiji — born 2 October 1869, Porbandar (Gujarat)
Gopal Krishna Gokhale advised Gandhiji — travel across India first, understand the people
Champaran Satyagraha — 1917, indigo farmers, Bihar; Gandhiji's first Indian Satyagraha
Non-cooperation movement — 1920-1922; constructive and negative programmes; suspended due to Chauri Chaura
Chauri Chaura incident — 5 February 1922, UP; mob burned police station, 22 policemen killed; Gandhiji suspended movement 12 February 1922
Civil Disobedience — Dandi March, 12 March 1930 to 6 April 1930; Salt March
Quit India Movement — August 1942; 'Do or Die'; mass movement
Gandhiji as people's leader — connected with masses, spoke their language, wore simple clothes
Second Round Table Conference — 1931, London; inconclusive because Congress-Muslim League disagreeement on separate electorates
Constituent Assembly — formation, members, key personalities
Objectives Resolution — presented by Jawaharlal Nehru (December 1946)
B.N. Rau — Constitutional advisor to Constituent Assembly
Hansa Mehta — demanded women's rights: equal rights, no discrimination, property rights
Govind Vallabh Pant — against separate electorates; argued it would weaken democracy and divide nation
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel — against separate electorates; argued similar to Pant
R.V. Dhulekar — aggressive plea for Hindi as constitutional language
N.G. Ranga — represented farmers/agriculturists in Constituent Assembly
Shrimati Durgabai — active in Constituent Assembly; women's rights
Indian Constitution — came into effect 26 January 1950 (NOT 15 August 1947)
Constitution enacted/adopted — 26 November 1949; came into force 26 January 1950
Direct Action Day — declared by Muslim League on 16 August 1946
Auxiliary/Subsidiary Alliance started by — Wellesley (relevant to earlier unit)

chapters.name: Madhya Pradesh — Historical Background
topics: MP as part of ancient Gondwana land — tribal culture flourished here
Prehistoric Stone Age civilization in MP — evidence from multiple sites
Bhimbetka — most important prehistoric site; approximately 500 caves; rock shelters with paintings
Bhimbetka cave paintings — daily life scenes: hunting, dancing, animals, battles; shows art of prehistoric man
Bhimbetka = Palaeolithic and Mesolithic culture important site
Other Stone Age sites in MP — Adamgarh (Hoshangabad), Awara, Indragarh (Mandsaur), Vidisha, Ujjain, Kayatha, Eran, Dangwala
Contribution of MP in National Movement — Kandel Nahr Satyagraha, Jhanda Satyagraha, Shastra Satyagraha
Key MP personalities in national movement — Dr. H.N. Katju, Pandit Sunderlal, Seth Govindas
Rupanathjee — rock inscription of Ashoka found at Rupnath (near Jabalpur), important for MP history

Agricultural fields incorporated in fortified area — reason: supply during siege
Therigatha — poems by Buddhist women monks

chapters.name: Delhi Sultanate (Travellers, Sufism, Bhakti)
important_topics: Al-Biruni — Kitab-ul-Hind (comparative method, Sanskrit texts translated); came with Mahmud Ghazni
Al-Biruni's distinctive structure in Kitab-ul-Hind — begins with a theory, then gives Indian and Greek views comparatively
Ibn Battuta — Moroccan, 'Rihla' book, came to India as qazi under Muhammad bin Tughlaq
Ibn Battuta's descriptions — coconut (nar-i-Hind), communication system (postal relay horses), Mughal cities
Bernier — French, came as physician to Dara Shikoh (later Aurangzeb), described Mughal cities as 'Camp Towns'
Bernier's Camp Towns description — because city without emperor moved with emperor's camp
Manucci — Italian, NOT the one who called cities 'Camp Towns' (Bernier did)
Alauddin Khilji — market control policy (4 markets, inspectors, price fixing)
Sufism — Islam mein mystical tradition, emphasized love for God
Chishti order — most popular in India; Shaikh Muinuddin Chishti (Ajmer), Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki (Delhi), Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi)
Khanqah — Sufi lodge/hospice, controlled by Sheikh/Pir
Rulers wanted Sufi support — legitimacy, spiritual blessings
Bhakti movement — Sant tradition, reached north India by 15th-16th century
Khalsa Panth — founded by Guru Gobind Singh (10th Guru), 1699 AD at Anandpur Sahib
Adi Granth Sahib — compiled by Guru Arjan Dev Ji
Nirguna Bhakti — Kabir (caste rejection), Guru Nanak (Sikhism root)
Saguna Bhakti — Mirabai (Krishna), Tukaram, Chaitanya
Nalayira Divya Prabandham — Tamil Vaishnav hymns by Alvars

chapters.name: Mughal Era
important_topics: Akbar — Mansabdari system (started in India by Akbar), Sulh-i-Kul (peace with all), Din-i-Ilahi
Mansabdari system — zat (personal rank), sawar (cavalry rank); 10 se 5000+ tak; ameer-ul-umara highest
Din-i-Ilahi — Akbar's new religion, combined elements of all religions; died with Akbar
Aurangzeb's Deccan policy — consequences: weakened empire, Maratha rise, treasury empty
Ain-i-Akbari — written by Abul Fazl, 3 parts, administrative details of Akbar's reign
Akbarnama — by Abul Fazl, Akbar's history
Mughal rural community — three constituents: zamindars, peasants (khud-kashta, pahi-kashta), village officials
Khud-kashta — resident peasants who owned land
Pahi-kashta — migrant peasants who cultivated others' land
Polaj — regularly cultivated land (best land)
Parauti — fallow for one or two seasons
Chachar — fallow for 3-4 years
Banjar — long-term fallow (5+ years)
Jins-i-kamil (perfect crops) — cotton and indigo; most profitable
Mawas — difficult/frontier tracts, outlaws and rebels took refuge here
Jama and Hasil in Mughal period — Jama = assessed revenue, Hasil = actual collection
Bernier — compared Mughal cities to camp towns, described sati, criticized Mughal land system
Bernier described sati practice — attracted by tragic element, women's choice vs. social pressure
Jajmani system — hereditary service exchange between castes in villages
Zabt system — method of revenue assessment by Todar Mal under Akbar

chapters.name: Maratha Power (Maratha Shakti)
important_topics: Rise of Maratha power — causes: geography of Maharashtra, religious awakening (Bhakti movement), guerrilla warfare, weakness of Deccan Sultans, linguistic unity, military experience, Shivaji's leadership
Shivaji — great nation-builder, born 1627; Ashta Pradhan system, Chauth, Sardeshmukhi
Ashta Pradhan — 8 ministers: Peshwa, Amatya, Mantri, Sachiv, Sumant, Senapati, Panditrao, Nyayadhish
Peshwa = Prime Minister (Pradhan Mantri) of Maratha state
Chauth — 1/4th (25%) of revenue collected from conquered areas
Sardeshmukhi — 10% extra revenue collected from entire kingdom
Battle of Haldighati (1576) — Maharana Pratap vs. Akbar's army; Pratap forced to retreat but never surrendered
Maharana Pratap — Sisodiya dynasty, fought lifelong against Mughal subjugation
Dr. Ashirvadilal Srivastava quote on Maratha rise — 200 years of preparation
Shivaji's guerrilla warfare — Mavala soldiers, hill forts strategy
Shivaji's character — skilled military commander, diplomat, administrator, religious tolerant

chapters.name: British Rule in India
important_topics: Battle of Plassey (1757) — British vs. Siraj-ud-Daula (Bengal Nawab); British won by deceit (Mir Jafar)
Battle of Buxar (1764) — British vs. Mir Kasim + Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II + Nawab of Awadh; British won
Treaty of Allahabad (1765) — terms: Diwani of Bengal, Bihar, Odisha to British; Shah Alam's pension; Awadh returned
Buxar significance > Plassey — Plassey gave indirect control, Buxar gave legal/formal control of India

Land Revenue Systems in India: (1) Permanent Settlement (Bengal, 1793, Cornwallis), (2) Ryotwari (Madras/Bombay, with individual farmers), (3) Mahalwari (Punjab/UP/Gangetic Plains, with village communities)
Fifth Report — submitted to British Parliament in 1813 (NOT 1815 — T/F trap!); about EIC administration
Subsidiary Alliance — started by Wellesley (NOT Cornwallis); rulers had to maintain British troops at their cost
Doctrine of Lapse — by Dalhousie; if no natural heir, state annexed by British
Dalhousie — Doctrine of Lapse; 'A cherry that will drop in our mouth one day' (about Awadh)
Cornwallis — Permanent Settlement in Bengal; Ryotwari system introduced later in Madras by Munro
Taluqdars — large landholders in Awadh; Taluqdar ka shhabdik arth = someone holding taluq (attachment)
Jotedars — powerful village-level landholders in Bengal; more powerful than Zamindars at local level
Zamindars — landholders under Permanent Settlement; had to pay fixed revenue or lose land
Awadh called Nursery of Bengal Army — because most sepoys came from Awadh; annexation 1856 caused resentment
Decline of Portuguese power in India — discipline lack, incompetent successors after Albuquerque, competition from Dutch/British/French
Cotton Supply Association — founded in Britain 1857 to reduce dependence on American cotton
Deccan Riots (1875) — against moneylenders; started in Poona/Indapur district
Sunset Law — land taken away at sunset if revenue not paid; oppressive revenue law

chapters.name: Resistance to British Rule (1857 and Tribal Revolts)
chapters.unit_name: Resistance to British Rule (1857 and Tribal Revolts)
important_topics: Revolt of 1857 — started 10 May 1857 from Meerut cantonment
Immediate cause — greased cartridges (pig and cow fat; offended both Muslims and Hindus)
Nature of 1857 revolt — debate: mere mutiny vs. first war of independence
John Lawrence, John Seeley — 'merely a military revolt'
V.D. Savarkar, Ashok Mehta — 'first war of Indian independence'
Main leaders of 1857: Rani Lakshmibai (Jhansi), Nana Sahib (Kanpur), Tantya Tope, Kunwar Singh (Bihar/Arrah), Begum Hazrat Mahal (Lucknow), Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah ('Danka Shah')
Rani Lakshmibai — 'Khoob lari mardani' — poem by Subhadra Kumari Chauhan
Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah — called 'Danka Shah' (drum king) for inspiring soldiers
Awadh called Nursery of Bengal Army — reason for revolt intensity there
British repression methods — new laws, disarming rebels, pardoning surrenderers early, military force
1857 revolt failure causes — premature start, limited area, no common goal, lack of resources, lack of organization
Rumours during 1857 revolt — why people believed: flour mixed with bone, cartridges greased, social anxiety
Rebels' unity efforts — appealing to common religion, declaring Bahadur Shah Zafar as leader, pamphlets
Santhal Revolt (1855-56) — against moneylenders, zamindars, British; leaders: Sidhu and Kanhu Manjhi
Santhal revolt causes — exploitation by dikus (outsiders), moneylenders, unfair land settlement
Manzil-abadi — Kanpur (location important for 1857)

chapters.name: National Movement (Rashtriya Andolan)
important_topics: Indian National Congress founding — 1885, A.O. Hume; initial objectives: protect Indian interests, national unity, NOT independence initially
Lal Bal Pal — Lala Lajpat Rai (Punjab), Bal Gangadhar Tilak (Maharashtra), Bipin Chandra Pal (Bengal) — Garam dal
Rise of extremist ideology causes — economic exploitation, Bengal partition, Lord Curzon's works, famine/plague, worldwide events
Bengal Partition — 1905, Lord Curzon — caused massive Swadeshi movement
Gandhiji — born 2 October 1869, Porbandar (Gujarat)
Gopal Krishna Gokhale advised Gandhiji — travel across India first, understand the people
Champaran Satyagraha — 1917, indigo farmers, Bihar; Gandhiji's first Indian Satyagraha
Non-cooperation movement — 1920-1922; constructive and negative programmes; suspended due to Chauri Chaura
Chauri Chaura incident — 5 February 1922, UP; mob burned police station, 22 policemen killed; Gandhiji suspended movement 12 February 1922
Civil Disobedience — Dandi March, 12 March 1930 to 6 April 1930; Salt March
Quit India Movement — August 1942; 'Do or Die'; mass movement
Gandhiji as people's leader — connected with masses, spoke their language, wore simple clothes
Second Round Table Conference — 1931, London; inconclusive because Congress-Muslim League disagreeement on separate electorates
Constituent Assembly — formation, members, key personalities
Objectives Resolution — presented by Jawaharlal Nehru (December 1946)
B.N. Rau — Constitutional advisor to Constituent Assembly
Hansa Mehta — demanded women's rights: equal rights, no discrimination, property rights
Govind Vallabh Pant — against separate electorates; argued it would weaken democracy and divide nation
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel — against separate electorates; argued similar to Pant
R.V. Dhulekar — aggressive plea for Hindi as constitutional language
N.G. Ranga — represented farmers/agriculturists in Constituent Assembly
Shrimati Durgabai — active in Constituent Assembly; women's rights
Indian Constitution — came into effect 26 January 1950 (NOT 15 August 1947)
Constitution enacted/adopted — 26 November 1949; came into force 26 January 1950
Direct Action Day — declared by Muslim League on 16 August 1946
Auxiliary/Subsidiary Alliance started by — Wellesley (relevant to earlier unit)

chapters.name: Madhya Pradesh — Historical Background
important_topics: MP as part of ancient Gondwana land — tribal culture flourished here
Prehistoric Stone Age civilization in MP — evidence from multiple sites
Bhimbetka — most important prehistoric site; approximately 500 caves; rock shelters with paintings
Bhimbetka cave paintings — daily life scenes: hunting, dancing, animals, battles; shows art of prehistoric man
Bhimbetka = Palaeolithic and Mesolithic culture important site
Other Stone Age sites in MP — Adamgarh (Hoshangabad), Awara, Indragarh (Mandsaur), Vidisha, Ujjain, Kayatha, Eran, Dangwala
Contribution of MP in National Movement — Kandel Nahr Satyagraha, Jhanda Satyagraha, Shastra Satyagraha
Key MP personalities in national movement — Dr. H.N. Katju, Pandit Sunderlal, Seth Govindas
Rupanathjee — rock inscription of Ashoka found at Rupnath (near Jabalpur), important for MP history
